newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns Americans in Cambodia 'Keep your head down'.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns Americans in Cambodia 'Keep your head down'.

text.p: The United States voiced deep concern on Monday over violence that has erupted in Cambodia and warned Americans in the Southeast Asian country to "keep your heads down."

"Our advice to American citizens in Phnom Penh right now is to keep your heads down, stay where you are, don't venture into the streets, because we can't assure anyone that fighting won't be starting again in the streets of Phnom Penh or in other cities in the country," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said at a briefing.

Some 40 students from Oklahoma were in Phnom Penh at one location and Burns said U.S. officials would try to help them leave if they wished to do so. He said a group of American Mormon students was also believed to be in Phnom Penh.

About 1,500 Americans are in Cambodia and there have been no reports of U.S. deaths or injuries from the fighting, Burns said. He urged Americans in Cambodia who did not feel safe in their homes to go to the Sofitel Cambodiana Hotel.

Burns said U.S. officials were "deeply concerned at the violence and loss of life" caused by the weekend conflict and called on authorities to prevent further violence. "We urge Cambodia's leaders to resolve their political differences peacefully and to abide by the principles of the Paris Peace Accords," he said.

Acting Secretary of State Thomas Pickering was meeting on Monday with ambassadors from the countries of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to assess "the political meaning of what happened over the weekend," Burns said.

After two days of fighting that may have left as many as 150 people dead, Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen took complete control of Phnom Penh and its outskirts as his ousted rival Prince Norodom Ranariddh vowed to organise resistance.

Asked to comment on statements by Hun Sen and the prince accepting Hun Sen's control of the capital, Burns said, "We prefer to continue our consultations with both political parties today in Phnom Penh and with our allies before we are able to make that kind of a final judgment that the Paris Peace Accords have been ruptured."

The 1991 accords were meant to end a civil war that began with the 1970 overthrow of the U.S.-backed Lon Nol government. They led to U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993 that brought about rule by two prime ministers who are sworn enemies.

Burns said he hoped the international community could agree to urge "political cooperation between the two co-prime ministers and their political parties so that the people of Cambodia do not have to live through a civil war."

ASEAN foreign ministers were to meet on Thursday in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, to discuss the crisis. Cambodia was to join ASEAN later this month along with Burma and Laos. Current members are Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
